title: Tenali Raman and the Royal Scarecrow
summary: A poor farmer named Venkat, whose modest sorghum fields bordered the royal hunting reserve, came to Tenali Raman in deep despair: 'Master Tenali, swarms of aggressive black crow...
full_text:
A poor farmer named Venkat, whose modest sorghum fields bordered the royal hunting reserve, came to Tenali Raman in deep despair:
'Master Tenali, swarms of aggressive black crows from the royal reserve descend upon my crops every dawn. I built scarecrows of straw with clay pots for heads, but the crows sit upon their shoulders and mock me! My family will starve if the grain is eaten!'

Tenali smiled: 'Fear not, Venkat. Tomorrow morning, thy field shall have the most formidable scarecrow in all of South India!'

Tenali went to the palace wardrobe and borrowed an old ceremonial royal mantle of embroidered crimson silk, a turban adorned with imitation peacock feathers, and an old painted wooden effigy used for military drill.
Tenali dressed the wooden figure in the King's royal robes and set it up in the center of Venkat’s sorghum field.

The next morning, King Krishnadevaraya rode past the fields on his morning hunt with his royal retinue.
The King stopped his horse in shock:
There, standing knee-deep in muddy sorghum, was an effigy dressed in his exact imperial robes, waving its sleeves in the wind, with two crows perched comfortably upon its royal turban, pecking at grains!

The King was furious:
'Who has committed this treasonous insult? Dressing a dirty scarecrow in the Emperor's royal robes?'

Tenali Raman stepped out from behind a hedge, bowing with exaggerated deference:
'Maharaj, pardon this humble farmer! He sought only the greatest power in the world to protect his crops!
He reasoned: "The entire empire of Vijayanagara trembles before the Emperor’s commands. Surely, if I dress my scarecrow as the King, the crows will flee in terror!"'

The King looked from Tenali’s innocent face to the crows happily pecking seeds atop the royal turban.
Tenali added gently:
'Alas, Your Majesty! The birds have taught us a profound political truth: royal robes and golden turbans mean nothing without the living mind of justice behind them. Even crows know the difference between an empty costume of power and true majesty!'

King Krishnadevaraya’s anger melted into appreciative laughter.
He ordered the royal granaries to compensate the farmer for all lost crops, and decreed that local farmers be provided with proper protective nets.
The King hugged Tenali, learning that true authority resides in wisdom, not in embroidered silk.
moral: A ruler who inspires true respect commands obedience, but relying merely on hollow symbols invites ridicule.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Crows and the Scarecrow"?
options: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.
